chapter: Road shows in the Southwest and Midwest
title: Managing a Tulsa theater, meeting Jelly Roll Morton and McCabe's Troubadours
summary: Spikes meets Jelly Roll Morton in Tulsa, then brings him to McCabe's Troubadours in Kansas where he plays overture and blackface comedy; Spikes returns to Los Angeles about 1912.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Pastime. On Second Avenue...Second Street in Muskogee, and we ran it for quite awhile. Then my brother went back East again, and I went to Muskogee, I mean to Tulsa and managed a theater there for a fellow for three or four months, and that's where I worked Jelly Roll Morton come through there, and he came by through there, and we got acquainted, and we got...kind of, you know ...close together. I liked his kind of style of (those)... music in those days, and I didn't know that I was ever going to be anything great or anything, so after a short while, my brother was with another show called McCabe's Troubadours in Kansas, and he sent for me again, so I went to Kansas, and we used to do a little musical act there then, and we stayed nine months in Kansas, jumping ten...twenty...thirty miles sometimes, and the railroad fare, I think, was two cents a mile and the whole twelve or fourteen people could jump for six or seven dollars--the whole show, baggage and all.
Well, I'm fixin' to tell you. And so this fellow was named McCabe, and he was...tried to...wanted to be a

comedian but he wasn't a comedian, but anyway, we had a nice little troupe. And so, after my brother and I got there, they had a girl piano player, and her husband was a drummer. That's all we had-- piano and drums--and they wanted some other people, and I got Jelly Roll, and I told him to come over there, and I thought he would work in the show, and when he came over there, he was doing blackface comedy, too. And he could play so much piano that, during the overture and everything, they would let him go out and play the overture, and the other girl would just play for the show, and he wasn't much of a comedian, but he was a great ragtime jazz piano player. My God, he was great! And anyway, he didn't stay long. He went, and we didn't stay long, so we came home--I did, and my brother went East, stayed awhile, and I came home around 1912, and I played saxophone around with little...this group...any group that when they got a job they'd call you for the job, and when you got a job, you'd call them. So that went on for three or four years, and I know that one day that I worked in the pictures, and they called me to get a band, and when I got a band together and went out there, it took me all day and a day-and-a-half nearly to get a piano player, then when I got out there, the piano didn't have no insides in it. It was a silent picture, and they just wanted somebody to sit at the piano, and I told them, "Well, I coulda brought anybody out here. Now I've been a coupla days trying to find a piano player." So that's the way it was.
